paper_title: AutoPILOT: A Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Multimodal foundation models can play video games well when the game waits for them, but often fail when it keeps running. We find that much of this gap lies in the harness, which decides what the model sees, what it remembers, and how its outputs become actions over time. Existing harnesses such as VISTA improve the first two, yet turn each model call into at most one action, so the agent acts only as often as its model thinks. We introduce AutoPILOT, which changes the third: in each model call, the model can send a primitive action, start an open-loop macro, or write a closed-loop controller that keeps playing from the screen without further model calls until it hands control back. To evaluate agents in real-time games, we build AFK-Bench, 120 diverse browser games grouped by how they respond to inaction and playable in real time or with the clock paused. With GPT-6.1 Sol under the same budgets, AutoPILOT reaches 68.6% real-time success against 38.3% for VISTA, and on GameWorld it keeps 80.0% in real time while VISTA drops from 84.1% to 42.9%. Its gains hold across models, and it reaches VISTA's final success rate at a fifth of its API cost. Our results suggest that how a harness turns model outputs into actions over time is a central yet underexplored part of agent design, and we hope AutoPILOT and AFK-Bench will serve as a foundation for agents in a world that does not wait.

Prior work has mostly refined the first two [11, 12, 36, 48, 57]. The third is usually left implicit, following the standard single-step agent loop [51] in which one model call yields at most one action and the environment is assumed to wait for it, as in ARC-AGI-3 or game benchmarks with settings that pause during inference [52, 54]. When the world keeps running, this default becomes bottleneck: the agent can act only as often as its model thinks, and on outdated frames (Fig. 1a). Letting the game clock run lowers VISTAs success rate on GameWorld [27] from 84.1% to 42.9%, gap also reported by Realtime-Bench [37] and for text-state agents [28]. Improving what the model sees and remembers does not remove it, as VISTA performs on par with the plain Codex harness in real time despite its visual memory and inspection tools (38.3% vs. 38.9%). Nor does more reasoning, which adds 47 points to VISTA at high effort. Much of the bottleneck lies in how the harness turns model outputs into actions. We introduce AutoPILOT, visual agent harness that changes the third aspect by letting one model call cover many environment steps. Like pilot with an autopilot, the model delegates routine control and takes over when called back. Each call chooses one of three execution modes (Fig. 1b). (1) primitive action is sent directly to the game. (2) An open-loop macro is sequence of actions written by the model. (3) closed-loop controller is short Python program that the model writes at run time. It reads the screen and acts about every 0.4 without further model calls. Control returns to the model on wake event: the macro or controller finishes, requests handoff, or meets screen it was not written for. Both the model and its controllers see screenshots, not the game state. To evaluate agents in real time, we introduce AFK-Bench (Away From Keyboard ), 120 browser games evenly divided into three types by what happens while the agent is idle. In hostile real-time environments, inaction risks failure. Benign real-time environments keep changing but do not punish inaction. Turnbased environments advance only when the agent acts. lost game restarts within fixed budgets of model calls, game time and environment steps. Every game can be played in real time or paused, and the difference measures what real time costs the agent. With the same model (GPT-6.1 Sol) and budgets, AutoPILOT succeeds in 68.6% of real-time episodes on AFK-Bench, against 38.3% for VISTA, and in 62.5% vs. 16.7% of hostile real-time ones. The gains hold with Claude Opus 5.5 and four further models, and AutoPILOT uses 47% fewer tokens and reaches VISTAs final success rate at 0.2 its API cost (Fig. 4d). sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Tab. 1 compares AutoPILOT with representative agents and harnesses, and Sec. gives an extended discussion. Harnesses for visual and game agents. Most agent harnesses follow ReAct [51], taking one action per reasoning step. Later work changes what the model sees or which tools it may call [20, 48]. On ARC-AGI-3 [3], VISTA [11] lifts the same models to perfect scores through visual memory and re-inspection of past frames. OpenVLHarness [57] adds visual tools and multimodal memory for static visual reasoning. Embodied agent frameworks and harnesses let general vision-language models act in simulated environments and control robots [6, 18, 49]. Computer-use agents [29, 46] and game agents [35, 36, 43] also act on screenshots. Most game agents, however, pause the game while the model generates, as do many game benchmarks [52] and the Lite setting of VideoGameBench [54]. These harnesses improve what the model sees or remembers, but assume that the world waits for it. Evaluation in real time. Latency is major reason why vision-language models fail at real-time games [54], and recent benchmarks keep the environment running during inference [15, 37, 39, 44]. Closest to ours, The World Wont Wait [28] compares paused and live clocks and finds that strong but slow model wins only when the game is paused. Its agents, however, read structured text states. Its TORSI method still calls model for every decision, with slow teacher guiding fast student. AutoPILOT acts on pixels and instead changes what one model call can do. Acting between model calls. Temporally extended actions date back to options [34]. Language models also write programs that serve as policies or skills [16, 19, 40, 41], but these programs mostly run on structured state in environments that wait. AutoHarness [22] refines code policy with environment feedback and resets offline, per game and for turn-based text games. Real-time agents pair slow 3 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay model with fast layer: reactive thread [44], concurrent inference coroutines [47], action chunks [4], options held until timer or repetition check fires [14], scripted executor over fixed macro actions [21], rule-based reflexes with latency charged to the simulation clock [56], or reflexes and policy trees compiled in advance [5, 9]. Asynchronous function calling lets returning call interrupt the model [10]. The most similar mechanism is DPT-Agent [55], in which the model writes condition rules at run time that steer hand-built state machine over the symbolic state of one game. In these systems, the fast path is mostly another model inference, code fixed in advance, or rules for game-specific executor. AsyncLLM can rewrite its coroutines, but only between evaluation rounds. AutoPILOT instead delegates acting to controllers that the model writes from pixels during the episode, including their perception, and interrupts them through wake events.

sections.title: 3 AutoPILOT
sections.content: AutoPILOT is developed on VISTA [11], which is built on the Codex harness, with additional tools for running macros and controllers in the background and wake events that return control to the model. As in VISTA, the model sees rendered frames together with the game clock and its remaining budgets, but never the game state or the DOM, from which only restart and decision-screen events are derived (Sec. B). AutoPILOT keeps VISTAs act tool, read-only tools (inspect, read pixels, history) and note files, so the two harnesses expose the same tools apart from delegation. All games share the same harness instructions and only the game description, task and controls differ. Sec. shows the full prompt, which adds budget rules, play tips and delegation rules to VISTAs instructions. AutoPILOT also reports the remaining budget after each tool result and notifies the model of restarts.

sections.title: 3.1 Acting in real time
sections.content: At time the agent can read frame o(t) and send an action: one keyboard or mouse event or an explicit wait, which counts as one environment step. The model is invoked in discrete model calls: call reads the frame at time tk and takes ℓk seconds, median of 6.1 for GPT-6.1 Sol at low effort. Existing visual harnesses turn each model call into one action, computed from o(tk) but executed at tk + ℓk. In real time this causes two problems: every action is ℓk seconds stale, so projectile that was safe in o(tk) may have arrived by then, and the agent acts at most once per model call. Pausing the clock removes both but changes the task. AutoPILOT instead lets single model call act over many steps, by starting macro or controller that keeps acting without further model calls. The model thus chooses how many steps each model call covers, and its actions no longer wait for the next call.

sections.title: 3.2 Three execution modes
sections.content: As shown in Fig. 1b, each model call may invoke one of three tools that act on the game. They differ in how long they act without the model and whether they read the screen. Primitive action (act). The model sends one action. act also stops any running macro or controller. Open-loop macro (run macro). The model writes sequence of actions, e.g. menu route learned from earlier interaction, and the worker sends them without looking. Closed-loop controller (python). The model writes short Python function run(api) that the worker executes for up to 120 in sandbox with one CPU, 1 GB of memory and no network access. Sec. gives the full setup. It reads frames with api.observe(), decides with ordinary code, and acts with api.act(). controller re-reads the frame and acts about every 0.4 with no model call. It can also ask the model for help through handoff, one of the wake events described in Sec. 3.3. Fig. 2 shows macro and controller from two recorded episodes.

sections.title: 3.3 Handing control back
sections.content: For delegation to be safe, control must return to the model once the running program no longer fits the situation. While macro or controller runs, the models tool call blocks: the model waits instead of 4 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay producing tokens, and the game is played by the worker. The call returns with fresh frame on one of six wake events: From the program. Handoff : the controller requests one with reason, e.g. on reaching goal or seeing something it was not written for. It may keep playing while the model reads the reason. Return: run ends at the stopping condition the model wrote or with an error. Macro done: all macro actions are sent. From the harness. Decision screen: the game waits for choice, such as in shop. Scene change: most of the screen differs from second earlier and then holds still. The harness then stops the program, since its plan may no longer fit. Timeout: the program has run for 120 s. game restart after loss affects the two modes differently. It stops running macro, which then returns and wakes the model. It does not wake the model while controller runs, since the controller observes an incremented reset epoch and can keep playing. Restarts do not pause the game: the next attempt starts at once, whether the model is thinking or program is running. running controller keeps playing it, and the model learns of the failure at its next wake event, where it can reflect and write revised controller. After waking, the model can keep, replace or stop (with act) the running controller. Thinking and acting overlap only after handoff, while the controller keeps playing and the model reads the reason. This overlap is small in practice (2.33.5% of inference time, Sec. F.3).

sections.title: 4 AFK-Bench
sections.content: AFK-Bench contains three environment types that vary the cost of inaction, and two clock protocols that play the same games in real time and paused, to test whether an agent acts well in real time. Games and tasks. AFK-Bench consists of 120 browser games, each with one task and an official success check, played in real browser. The games span shooters, platformers, arcade and action games, puzzles and board-like games. Sec. describes how we collected them from public game sites and validated each with 13 scripted checks. Success and progress are computed from the game state by the benchmarks evaluator. This state is never exposed to the agent, which sees only rendered frames plus restart and decision-screen events (Sec. B). Environment types. We divide the games into three types of 40 by what happens when the agent does nothing. To assign each game, scripted probe stops all actions for 60 and checks whether the attempt fails, the world keeps changing, or nothing happens. Fig. 3 shows three example games of each type, together with how often VISTA and AutoPILOT win them in real time. Hostile real-time environments, where inaction risks failure: an idle agent loses the attempt, health or life. In the shooter Praxis Fighter X, ship that does not dodge is destroyed within seconds. Figure 3 The three environment types of AFK-Bench. Each row shows three of the 40 games of one type. Below each game are the real-time wins of VISTA and AutoPILOT out of three episodes with GPT-6.1 Sol. Tab. 8 lists all 120 games. Benign real-time environments, where the world keeps moving but inaction causes no direct harm: an idle agent loses time, not the attempt, as in Tiny Truck Racing. 5 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay Turn-based environments, where the game changes only when the agent acts and no countdown runs, as in the box-pushing puzzle Trichromat. The types thus separate two costs of slow thinking: in hostile real-time environments it causes failure, while in the other two it only wastes time and budget. Sec. details the probe, including second probe for games whose danger appears only after some play. Clock protocols. Every game can be played under two clock protocols. In real time, the game clock never stops: the game keeps running during each model call, as for human player who looks away from the keyboard. Under the paused clock, the harness freezes the game from the start of each model call until it ends, together with any running macro or controller. Game time therefore passes only while no model call is in progress. Every game becomes turn-based for the agent, with no time pressure while the model thinks. Under both protocols, the games own pause and restart controls are blocked, so the agent cannot stop the clock itself. The drop from the paused clock to real time measures how much an agent loses to its own latency. Budgets. An episode ends with win, the games own end, or when one of its budgets is used up: 100 model calls, 2000 of game time or 2000 environment steps. model call is one invocation of the model, which issues at most one tool call (a reply without one also counts). An environment step is one action sent to the game, whether by act, macro or controller. single-step harness thus spends one model call per step and sends at most 100 steps, so only the call and time budgets bind it, whereas one AutoPILOT model call can launch macro or controller that sends many steps, and the step budget caps these. In real time, thinking time counts as game time, while loading and automatic restarts do not. After loss, the game restarts within the same budgets, so the agent can try again. Metrics. Our main metric is the success rate (SR): the fraction of episodes in which the games official success check fires before any budget is used up. Because an episode can span several attempts, SR measures whether an agent wins within its budgets, possibly after earlier losses. Sec. 5.3 also reports success on the first attempt. The mean progress (PG) gives finer signal. It averages over episodes the highest progress reached in any attempt, which the evaluator normalizes to [0, 1] for each game. We also report the number of model calls, tokens and API cost per episode.

sections.title: 5 Experiments
sections.content: We aim to answer four questions: how much single-step harness loses when the world keeps running and whether AutoPILOT recovers it (Sec. 5.2), where the gains come from (Sec. 5.3), how they scale with budget, effort and speed (Sec. 5.4), and whether they generalize (Sec. 5.5).

sections.title: 5.2 Main results
sections.content: AutoPILOT outperforms existing harnesses. As Tab. 2 shows, AutoPILOT nearly doubles the real-time success rate of existing harnesses: 68.6% against 38.3% for VISTA and 38.9% for Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol, and 53.3% against 30.0% and 32.5% for VISTA and Claude Code with Claude Opus 5.5, while costing $0.89 per episode against $1.50 for VISTA with GPT-6.1 Sol (Tab. 4). The margin is largest in hostile real-time environments (62.5% vs. 16.7% with GPT-6.1 Sol) and remains large in the other two types. Of the 360 paired GPT-6.1 Sol episodes, 111 are won only by AutoPILOT and 2 only by VISTA. Memory and perception tools bring no overall gain. In real time, VISTA performs no better than the plain Codex and Claude Code harnesses (38.3% vs. 38.9% with GPT-6.1 Sol, 30.0% vs. 32.5% with Claude Opus 5.5), despite its lossless visual memory and inspection tools. Each VISTA action is computed from frame about one model call old, so better view of it cannot help. Even with the clock paused, these tools add 4.4 points over Codex (56.1% vs. 51.7%) and none over Claude Code (39.2% vs. 42.5%). AutoPILOT is less sensitive to the game clock. Moving from the paused clock to real time lowers the success rate of VISTA and Codex by 17.8 and 12.8 points with GPT-6.1 Sol, but that of AutoPILOT by 4.5. The drops are closer with Claude Opus 5.5 (9.2 and 10.0 for VISTA and Claude Code, 7.5 for AutoPILOT), while on GameWorld VISTA loses 41.2 points and AutoPILOT only 2.9 (Sec. 5.5).

sections.title: 5.3 Why AutoPILOT wins
sections.content: We analyze the gap in three steps: gains beyond latency, the responsible component, and recovery from failures. Gains beyond latency. Even with the clock paused, where no action is stale, AutoPILOT beats VISTA by 17.0 points with GPT-6.1 Sol and 21.7 with Claude Opus 5.5, so latency explains only part of the gap. The rest comes from executing whole plan per model call instead of single action, which makes far better use of the model-call budget. VISTA spends one model call on each action, so long action sequences use up its budget: 208 of its 222 real-time failures end by exhausting its 100 calls, after only 78 steps per episode. AutoPILOT instead sends 681 steps from 43 model calls, about 16 per call, because one macro or controller carries out many steps. The model also chooses the mode that fits the game (Tab. 3): controllers send 98% of the steps in hostile real-time and 89% in benign real-time environments, whereas in turn-based environments, which allow planning ahead, macros account for 36% of calls and 26% of steps. Which component is responsible. Tab. 4 removes the two delegation tools, python and run macro, one at time (seeds in Tab. 10). sections.title: 5.5 Generalization to GameWorld
sections.content: We also evaluate both harnesses on GameWorld [27], whose 170 tasks in 34 browser games do not overlap with AFK-Bench, using the same budgets (Tab. 6). With the clock paused, the two harnesses are close (84.1% vs. 82.9% with GPT-6.1 Sol), as GameWorld tasks are short enough that VISTA rarely runs out of calls (3 of its 27 failures). In real time, however, VISTA loses 41.2 points with GPT-6.1 Sol and 25.9 with Claude Opus 5.5, while AutoPILOT loses only 2.9 and 4.7. The robustness of AutoPILOT to the game clock carries over to different set of games. 10 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented AutoPILOT, visual agent harness in which the model delegates acting to macros and controllers that it writes at run time. Because each model call can launch whole plan rather than single action, AutoPILOT substantially outperforms existing harnesses in real time at lower cost, across models and on two benchmarks, without any training. Our results suggest that how model outputs become actions over time deserves as much attention in harness design as what the model sees and remembers, for game agents and agents operating live interfaces or robots.

sections.title: A Extended related work
sections.content: Agent harnesses. harness is the code around model that turns the environment into the models observations and the models outputs into actions. ReAct [51] interleaves reasoning with one action per turn. SWE-agent [48] shows that the interface given to the model matters as much as the model. CodeAct [41] lets single action be program that calls many tools. VISTA [11] perceives the game as images, keeps every frame in lossless visual memory and lets the model re-inspect frames as it reasons, raising the ARC-AGI-3 score of the same model from 40.68 to 100. Our episodes restart after loss, so the model can reflect on failed attempts as in Reflexion [31]. Computer-use and game agents. Vision-based computer-use agents ground actions in screenshots [7, 23, 29, 46]. Game agents range from reinforcement-learning policies trained per game [24] to foundationmodel agents that play many games from pixels or structured state [32, 33, 36, 40, 42, 43]. Lumine [35] trains vision-language model to play 3D open-world games in real time. It reads frames at 5 Hz, emits actions at 30 Hz and reasons only when needed. It reaches real-time play through training, whereas AutoPILOT uses general model without training. Real-time evaluation. VideoGameBench [54] reports latency as major failure cause for vision-language models. Real-Time Reasoning Gym [44] and ROAR [39] advance their environments during inference. Realtime-Bench [37] evaluates 30 web and 20 game tasks from screenshots under wall, paused and token clocks with one-action-per-model-call harness. Win Fast or Lose Slow [15] adapts model size and quantization to the time pressure. The World Wont Wait [28] evaluates 180 tasks from six game types. It uses structured text observations and game-specific action interfaces. Several of these plan ahead, such as button plans in Mario and flap schedules in Bird. While model call is pending, the previous control stays active. Acting while thinking. AgileThinker [44] runs reactive and planning thread in parallel, and SwiftSage [20] pairs small fine-tuned model with large one, in the spirit of dual-process theories [13]. AsyncLLM [47] is general framework for asynchronous inference rather than game agent, and it is evaluated mainly on streaming video understanding. In two ViZDoom scenarios, background thinker sets course of action that fast coroutine turns into per-frame actions from the two latest frames. An appendix experiment lets the agent rewrite its own coroutines between evaluation rounds. Real-time chunking [4] executes one action chunk of robot policy while the next is generated. Dong et al . [9] show that GUI agents often choose correctly but act too late. They pre-compile guarded policy trees sized to the decoding latency, which raises success within the decision window from 0.50 to 0.79. Their branches are enumerated in advance for discrete GUI states, whereas AutoPILOTs model writes closed-loop programs for continuous games at run time. TypeGo [5] runs planning loops at several timescales and has an LLM compile reflexes offline into Python condition and action functions that run at 100 Hz. AutoPILOT synthesizes its controllers at run time from the current screen.

sections.title: B Harness details
sections.content: Tools. Tab. 7 lists the tools available to the model in each harness. AutoPILOT keeps VISTAs act and read-only tools and adds run macro and python, which together give the three execution modes of Sec. 3.2. Actions. Every action, whether sent by act, macro or controller, uses one schema. Its types are wait, press key, press keys, type, click, click hold, mouse move, drag and scroll. The action press key holds one key, and press keys holds two keys at once but rejects opposing directions. The action type enters up to five characters. Each action is one environment step. Coordinates refer to the 1280 720 screenshot, durations are at most 2 s, and the default hold or wait is 0.4 s. Only the keys of the games declared controls are allowed. 15 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay

sections.content: act (one action per call) run macro (open-loop) python (closed-loop controller) inspect, read pixels, history notes (GUIDE.md, WORKING.md) Table 7 Game tools per harness in the GPT-6.1 Sol runs. Every harness sees screenshot after each action, and AutoPILOT also on every wake. The Codex harness also has screenshot and keeps Codexs code execution without shell, file or network access. Macros. run macro takes list of at most 200 actions and sends them in order without reading the screen. With the default on reset: stop, game restart stops the macro. With continue, the list restarts on the new attempt. Controller API. controller is function run(api) that background worker executes for at most 120 s. It runs in Docker sandbox with one CPU, 1 GB of memory, 60 of CPU time, no network and no access to the game or host files. Python, NumPy and run macro helper are available. api.observe() returns the latest frame as 720 1280 3 RGB array together with the public state: the game clock, the remaining budgets and reset epoch. api.act(action) sends one action in the format above, which counts as one step toward the step budget. api.request handoff(reason) wakes the model while the controller keeps running. Returning from run ends the controller and also wakes the model. api.notify reset(reason) records game restart, signalled by an incremented reset epoch, without waking the model. new controller replaces the running one, and act stops it. There is no fixed control rate: controller observes and acts as fast as its own code and action durations allow. In practice it acts about every 0.4 s. Waiting and waking. After run macro or python call, the harness holds the tool result while the macro or controller runs, so the model produces no tokens in the meantime. It polls every 0.25 for one of the wake events of Sec. 3.3. The result is released with fresh frame on handoff, when the program ends, stops or times out, or when the episode ends. Screen watch. Each macro and controller has screen watch, which raises the scene-change wake event and which the model can tune or turn off per call. scene change fires when at least half of the screen differs from the frame about one second earlier and the new screen then holds for three frames, so flash or continuous motion does not trigger it. An optional static check fires when the screen stays unchanged for 10 while actions are sent. On trigger the watch stops the program by default. It can instead only wake the model. Signals derived from the game state. No harness reads the game state, but two kinds of events derived from it reach the agent. Automatic restarts. After loss, AutoPILOTs controllers see an incremented reset epoch, and the model receives one-line notice that the attempt failed and the game restarted. Codex receives only this notice, and VISTA receives the last frame before the restart. Decision screens. Four of the 120 tasks, all hostile real-time, declare game states in which the game waits for choice. In real time, AutoPILOT and Codex poll the game state every 0.25 s. When such screen appears, the running controller is stopped and the model receives neutral notice. VISTA receives no such notice. No harness receives it with the clock paused. Removing the four tasks changes the real-time gap between AutoPILOT and VISTA from +30.3 to +30.2 points with GPT-6.1 Sol and from +23.3 to +21.6 with Claude Opus 5.5.

sections.title: C Prompt
sections.content: Each prompt starts with the games description, task and controls, which are shared by all harnesses. VISTA then receives its official instructions, with one added sentence in real time: Real time continues 16 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay while you think and while tools run; the game is not paused between your actions. AutoPILOT receives the same text followed by the rules block below, shown in its real-time version for the GPT-6.1 Sol runs. The prompts are reproduced verbatim and call environment steps game inputs. Under the paused clock, the first paragraph instead states that the game is paused while the model thinks, and the last rule that running controller is paused while the model thinks. # Real-time play The game keeps running while you think, call tools, and run Python. ## Budget and ending - You have 2000 seconds of game time. Loading and automatic restarts are not counted. - You can make at most 100 tool calls; response without tool call also counts as one. Actions sent by your running controller do not count toward this limit. All game inputs together are limited to 2000. - response without tool call is submitted as final answer and the episode continues. Only the game decides success. ## Choosing tool - Use act for single inputs: starting, quick reactions and recovery. - Calling act stops running controller. - Use run_macro for short sequence whose effect you have already seen. - Use python for controller that keeps playing from the screen while you think. Prefer run_macro when it is enough. - Test an uncertain control briefly before you rely on it for longer. - Decide what visible change counts as progress. Motion on screen and passing time are not progress. - Let controller keep running while you think only if it is already working. Otherwise have it hand control back and stop. The Codex harness receives no instructions of ours beyond the game text and the following rules: - The game runs in real time. It does not pause while you think or use tools. - You have 2000 seconds of game time. Loading and automatic restarts are not counted. - You can send at most 100 responses. Each screenshot or act call counts as one response, and so does reply with no tool call. - You can send at most 2000 game inputs. Each act is one input, including waits. - reply with no tool call is submitted as final answer and the episode continues; it also uses one game input. The episode ends only on success, game end or budget end. Later runs of AutoPILOT add three rules and end every tool result with budget line such as Budget left: 1999 of 2000 game inputs, 99 of 100 responses, 1989 of 2000 game time. - Each act, each run_macro action and each api.act call uses one game input, including waits. response without tool call can also use one game input. Other tools and api.observe() use none. - If any budget remains, keep playing: try different approach instead of giving final answer. - Combine several waits, clicks or key presses into one run_macro call: each tool call uses one of your 100 responses. sections.title: D Baselines
sections.content: VISTA runs its official GameWorld profile and tools through the Codex app server of Codex CLI 0.159.2, like AutoPILOT. Its budget is 100 tool calls plus 2000 of game time. Every tool call counts, including inspect, read pixels, history and the note tools. The Codex harness runs Codexs own base instructions, agent loop and context compaction in single thread per episode. Web search, browser and computer use, skills, plugins and sub-agents are disabled. Its code execution has no shell, file system or network access. The Claude Code harness runs Claude Codes default system prompt and agent loop with act and screenshot as its only tools. All built-in tools are disabled, and context-compaction turns do not count as model calls. The no-op agent sends no step from the start of an episode to its end, with the same automatic restarts and the same evaluator. Each episode runs for 600 of game time. It wins no task. Its mean progress is .079 in hostile real-time environments and at most .002 in the other two, consistent with the type assignment of Sec. 4. The random agent sends uniformly random valid step as fast as the harness allows, at median of 2.9 steps per second. It runs one episode per task, within 2000 steps and 2000 s. It wins 5.8% of tasks, mostly in hostile real-time environments, where it wins 10.0%. It raises mean progress over the no-op agent by .234 on paired tasks, so progress is best read against this floor. 17 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay

sections.title: E Benchmark details
sections.content: Games. The 120 games run offline in pinned Chromium image. Of these, 37 are built with HTML5 canvas, 21 with PICO-8, 22 with Unity WebGL, 17 with Flash through the Ruffle emulator, 13 with Godot, 9 with other WebAssembly engines and 1 with Phaser. Each game exposes its state to the evaluator through small per-game adapter, which the agent cannot access. None of the 34 games of GameWorld is among them. We collected and wrapped all 120 games ourselves from freely playable web games. The manifest records the source page of 111 of them and pins every game file by its hash. Of these pages, 94 are on itch.io, 10 on Armor Games, 3 on Kongregate, 3 on Newgrounds and 1 on Not Doppler. Tab. 9 lists each games author, source and licence. Eight games carry licence stated by their author. The other 112 games state no licence, so we treat their terms as unknown. Selection. From pool of 568 collected games, each game was assigned an environment type from its description and idle probes. task was admitted only after scripted acceptance test that uses no model and runs with the same code and browser image as the reported runs. Its 13 checks test whether scripted policy can win in real time. They also require that pausing through either harness stops the game clock and that resuming restores normal speed. Score, prompt and screen must agree, the game must show no undeclared freeze, and failures and restarts must be detected. Memory must stay within its limit, and 60 of idling must cause no penalty in turn-based games but must cause one in hostile real-time games. The games own pause must be blocked, and phases the agent cannot control must be recognized. The budget must be feasible, the prompt must name only allowed keys, and the game state must be sampled at regular rate. The 120 tasks were frozen before any run reported here. For games whose danger appears only after some play, second probe first plays scripted policy for up to 120 and then idles for 60 s. Episode rules. All runs block the games own pause and restart controls. From the moment game reports failure until it is playable again, all actions are discarded but still counted as steps, including those of running controller. This time does not count as game time, and neither does loading or an automatic restart. Phases the agent cannot control, such as automatic cutscenes, do not count as game time either. wall-clock safety cap of 4000 ends any episode. Every real-time episode is audited against the games own clock for pauses. An episode is scored by the benchmarks evaluator only. run that fails for infrastructure reasons is retried automatically and not scored. used-up budget is failure. model response that takes longer than the per-call deadline of 300 s, or request that the model provider rejects as too large, counts as failure of the episode. Table 21 Three recorded episodes with GPT-6.1 Sol in real time. Times are game time. Hand-picked illustrations, not from the main-table runs. Radius Raid: enough skill, not enough time. In this hostile real-time game, VISTA strafes once per model call and reaches 88% of the goal by 3:26, as Fig. 9 shows. But enemies drain its health while it thinks, and it fails 12 times. Every restart resets progress, so its 100 model calls run out at 10:24 with best progress of 90%. AutoPILOT turns on autofire with one act, and its first controller fails to send actions. The model reads the failure from the next frame and writes second controller that segments the ship and the enemies by color, aims at the nearest enemy and orbits the arena while avoiding contact. Then the model waits. The controller takes 58 of the episodes 59 steps and reaches the goal at 1:02, after three model calls and without failure. Trichromat: enough time, not enough model calls. Waiting costs nothing in this turn-based puzzle, so latency is not the problem. The problem is the model-call budget, as Fig. 10 shows. VISTA spends one model call per move and solves two of the three rooms, at 3:06 and 9:10, before its 100th call arrives in the last room. AutoPILOT writes the first room as Python model and searches it before moving, tests the first move of the 25-move solution with act, and executes the rest with one controller. When its model of the second room has no solution, it tests the unknown mechanic, floor button that opens 30 AutoPILOT: Visual Agent Harness for Real-Time Gameplay door, revises the model, and again executes the plan in bulk. It solves all three rooms by 3:16 with 14 model calls. Controllers and one macro take 180 of its 182 steps.

sections.title: H Limitations
sections.content: AutoPILOT relies on model-written perception and control code, which is easier in 2D browser games than in cluttered 3D scenes. In hostile real-time environments most of its wins come after restart, so winning an unseen real-time game at the first attempt remains open. Models also rarely let controller keep playing after handoff, and doing so by default did not add wins, as Sec.
